passage:
After Jonas told her by the bike racks that he just wanted to be friends, Astrid cycled home through the sleet in Gothenburg without her gloves. She didn't text him. She didn't post anything. She sat at her desk with her grandmother's old notebook and wrote until her hand cramped. A poem about a lighthouse that nobody visited. Another about the bike racks, with every bike leaving but one.
On Saturday, her friend Ingrid read them at the kitchen table over cinnamon buns. "These are really good," Ingrid said quietly. "Sad, but good."
Astrid looked at the page. It still hurt. But the hurt had edges now, a shape she could hold up and show someone. That evening she signed up for the school poetry night.

qa.q: What did Astrid's first poem describe?
qa.a: A lighthouse that nobody visited.

qa.q: Why did Astrid write instead of texting Jonas or posting something?
qa.a: She was hurt, and writing let her give the pain a shape without lashing out at him or exposing it online.

qa.q: Which choice turned Astrid's pain into something she could share?
qa.a: Letting Ingrid read the poems, and then signing up for the poetry night, so others could see the feeling she had shaped.

qa.q: What might it have meant to Ingrid to read the poems?
qa.a: Ingrid got to understand how much Astrid was hurting without having to ask, and could answer with honest, gentle praise.

grounding: A teenager in Sweden turned down by a boy writes poems instead of lashing out, and sharing them gives her hurt a shape.

passage:
The school magazine box sat outside the library, and Maria walked past it three times on Monday. Last week Neil had laughed when her friend passed him her note, and said "No thanks" loud enough for half of Class 10 to hear. Maria hadn't said a word to him since. She hadn't cried at school either. Instead, every free period, she sat in the library corner filling a notebook: a song about a bus stop, a poem about a door that only opened one way.
On Monday she tore out the door poem and dropped it into the box. Two weeks later, Simran Ma'am called her to the staff room. "This one's going on page four," she said. "It's honest." Maria went pink, and then, for the first time in days, she smiled.

qa.q: Where did Maria drop the door poem?
qa.a: Into the school magazine box outside the library.

qa.q: Why did Maria fill a notebook instead of saying anything to Neil?
qa.a: She was hurt and embarrassed after the public 'No thanks', and writing gave the pain a shape without lashing out.

qa.q: Which choice was the turning point for Maria, and what came of it?
qa.a: Tearing out the door poem and putting it in the magazine box; it let others see her feeling and brought Simran Ma'am's praise.

qa.q: How might Simran Ma'am see the door poem?
qa.a: She sees honest writing worth publishing, and may sense real feeling behind it without needing to know the story.

grounding: A teenager publicly turned down at school writes poems and songs instead of lashing out, and one is chosen for the school magazine.

passage:
Dear Pallavi,
You asked if I'm okay after Vivek said he "didn't feel that way". Honestly? The first night I wanted to message him something horrible. I even typed it. Then I deleted it and wrote a song instead. It's called "Seen at 9:42", because that's when he read my message and didn't reply. It's only four lines and a chorus, but when I sang it to myself on the terrace, I cried, and it felt... cleaner? Like the feeling had somewhere to live that wasn't my stomach.
I've written six poems since. One is funny, about me practising in the mirror what I'd say to him. I'm sending you two. Please don't show anyone. Okay, maybe show your brother.
Love,
Your cousin-sister Himani

qa.q: What is Himani's song called?
qa.a: "Seen at 9:42".

qa.q: What did Himani feel on the first night, and how did the song change it?
qa.a: She was hurt enough to want to send something horrible; singing the song let her cry and made the feeling 'cleaner', as if it had somewhere to live.

qa.q: What choice on the first night made the difference?
qa.a: Deleting the horrible message and writing a song instead, which turned the hurt into something she could shape and share.

qa.q: What might Pallavi feel on receiving the two poems?
qa.a: Trusted and relieved that Himani is coping, and perhaps touched to be let into something so private.

grounding: A teenage girl writes to her cousin that after a rejection she deleted a cruel message and wrote a song and poems instead.

passage:
Jyoti, you asked why I've been scribbling in every free period. Okay. Remember Kabir? After farewell practice I finally told him I liked him. He said, "You're a really good friend, Ankita," and walked back to the others. Friend. That word sat on me for days.
I wanted to post something mean about him. I had it typed. Then I thought, no, I'll write how it actually feels. So I did. In Hindi, because it hurt in Hindi. Eleven lines about waiting at the bus stop for a message that doesn't come.
Yesterday Ma'am read it and asked if she could put it in the school magazine, without names. And you know what's strange? Now that it's on paper, it doesn't feel like it's only mine. Riya from 9C came up and said, "That's exactly it."

qa.q: What did Kabir say after farewell practice?
qa.a: "You're a really good friend, Ankita."

qa.q: Why did Ankita decide to write instead of posting the mean message?
qa.a: Ankita wanted to say how it actually felt rather than hurt Kabir, and writing let the pain come out honestly without lashing out.

qa.q: What turning point changed how the heartbreak felt?
qa.a: Deleting the typed post and writing the eleven lines in Hindi; once the poem was on paper and shared, the pain had a shape and others could recognise it.

qa.q: What does Riya's "That's exactly it" suggest about how the poem reached others?
qa.a: Riya seems to have felt something similar, so the poem turned a private hurt into something shared and less lonely 🙂

grounding: Shows a teenager rejected by a classmate choosing to write a poem instead of a mean post, giving the hurt a shape that others can see and share.

passage:
I'm Nikita, Gautam's neighbour on the third floor. We've walked to tuition together since Class 6, so I noticed when Gautam went quiet after Sneha said no to him at the Holi party. He didn't rant, didn't block her, didn't say one bad thing about her to anyone.
Instead, every evening I heard his old keyboard through the wall: the same few notes, over and over, and his voice trying words, stopping, trying again. His notebook, which used to be all physics, filled up with short lines crossed out and rewritten.
Three weeks later he played the song at our building's Sunday music evening. It was about a coloured handprint fading from a sleeve. He didn't look at anyone while he sang. Afterwards two aunties hugged him, and a boy from the fifth floor asked for the words.
I don't know if it hurt less. But he looked lighter.

qa.q: What was Gautam's song about?
qa.a: A coloured handprint fading from a sleeve.

qa.q: What might Gautam have been feeling as he tried the words over and over?
qa.a: He was likely hurt by Sneha's no, and shaping it into a song gave the pain somewhere to go instead of turning it on her.

qa.q: Which choice after the Holi party worked well for Gautam?
qa.a: Not ranting or blocking Sneha but writing and rewriting the song, then sharing it, which gave the hurt a form others could see.

qa.q: Why might the boy from the fifth floor ask for the words?
qa.a: The song may have matched something the boy felt too, showing how Gautam's private hurt became something others could hold on to.

grounding: Illustrates, through a neighbour's eyes, a rejected teenager who turns heartbreak into a song instead of lashing out, and shares it with others.
